newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU single tax plans seen part of larger policy row.
newsitem.headline: EU single tax plans seen part of larger policy row.

text.p: The idea of tax harmonisation for nations joining a single European currency is causing dismay among some officials who see it as a futile attempt to appease French demands for more centralised economic decision-making.

The controversial plan, part of an ongoing debate over "flexibility" which would allow some EU countries to move ahead with integration without being held back by others, is being studied by the European Commission, the EU's executive.

Under the guidance of EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, a Frenchman, the Commission is in the midst of preparing a study that looks into the issue of harmonisation of indirect taxes such as VAT.
But EU officials, including some within the Commission, expressed dismay over the proposal which for some seemed to come out of the blue.
Mario Monti, European Commissioner for the single market, told Reuters on Monday that flexibility was not the preferred route towards tax harmonisation.
Others said it could become a device which could fracture relations within the EU, pitting a hard-core group within economic and monetary union (EMU) against those outside.
"It's a non-issue," said one senior EU monetary official. "The only way I can understand it is that it plays into what the French want on economic policy."

France, long-wedded to interventionist economic policies, has stepped-up the pressure for an informal, Group of Seven-like council of ministers to oversee the policies of a future European central bank (ECB).
Wary that the ECB would be too narrowly focused on battling inflation, French officials have said they plan to make such a council one of their priorities in the months ahead.

Some officials saw de Silguy's study on taxes as a step towards appeasing Paris and diffusing what could be a serious row among member governments. Apart from that many were at a loss for alternative explanations.
"I'm not aware of any serious thought being given to this at the national capitals," said another official.

While the Commission has played down the divisive aspects of such a strategy, stressing that such a development should not be seen as a new precondition for a single currency, analysts say there is nothing to prevent countries inside EMU from embracing closer harmony on taxes.
Moreover, such harmonisation could de-facto become an additional hurdle for future participants in monetary union.

"If you have EMU and they decide we need to have a common 15 percent withholding tax, the next country to join will be asked to do the same thing," said Daniel Gros, economist at the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels.

Gros reckoned that it would make sense for a single currency bloc to have a common approach towards taxes on interest income, for example, but was a less than enthusiastic about income or corporate tax harmonisation.
Other analysts, however, said a gradual move towards single taxation on all fronts was inevitable given the EU's recent agreement on a budget stability pact for countries inside EMU.
Such a pact would fine governments running annual budget deficits above three percent of total output, a constraint which in practice would limit the tax policy options governments could employ.
"Under a stability pact I find it very difficult to see fiscal policies and tax rates all that different," said Vicky Pryce, chief economist at KPMG Management Consulting in London.

The chief irony of such an outcome, she added, was that countries like Britain, which are in favour of "flexibility" in EU integration, might find themselves facing policy decisions among EMU members which they do not like.
